cells.tense: You are the one who says the good news out loud and brings people into it right now.
cells.ask: Pick one ordinary thing that went well this week and say it out loud to two people before the week ends — a message, a call, a drink, no event required.
cells.core:
Good news doesn't stop with you. When something lands, your first move is to bring it to someone — the message, the plan, the night it gets said in company — and the evening comes alive for it. People arrive as they are and no audition is required, which is not the usual arrangement. You can hold a group in your attention without needing it to look a certain way.

So don't overbuild this. What gets said out loud in company becomes a thing people remember together, and that memory keeps a group from drifting. This week, notice the specific pleasure of telling rather than keeping. You are already built for it — the telling is happening, and you get to be in the room for it.
cells.sheetLine: You bring good news into the room, not just to yourself.
cells.handle: You get to be in the room for it.

cells.tense: You are already braced for the turnout that has not happened, turning the joy into work ahead of time.
cells.ask: Work out the smallest version of the gathering that would still honestly count, and let it happen this week before you're sure it will land — one friend, one walk, no event.
cells.core:
The moment gets stepped around. Every good thing acquires a future: whether it'll land, who might not show, what it should look like, what it says about the group if it doesn't. The bracing sits where the celebration was going to be, and the joy keeps getting rehearsed instead of felt. Nobody asked for the report.

The fix is small. Gather less, and gather it before it's proved. One friend, one plain good thing, one hour with no verdict required afterward. A play you wait on until it is safe is a play that doesn't get made. Send the message tonight rather than after the schedule clears.

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door that has closed, waiting for the group to come back for you.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you'd normally keep quiet and say it to two people this week — a small win, a good day, one thing you're looking forward to — without building a case for it first.
cells.core:
The aliveness stays private. You show up for other people's news and keep your own filed away — not that there is nothing to say, only that saying it does not reach anyone right now. You are not short on joy. You are short on letting it land where it can be met.

Start where the fear isn't. Let one good thing reach one person before you have weighed whether they deserve it. This runs on contact, and contact is the part currently missing. Small and spoken beats big and kept, so give it something small to carry this week and see what the room does with it.

cells.tense: You are already convening people around what matters, and the pen is down in a room you are already writing in.
cells.ask: Catch one thing you do as just how the group runs — a dinner someone hosts, a chat someone starts, a message someone sends — and claim it out loud this time, once.
cells.core:
You are the one keeping something alive. The dinners, the group chat, the birthdays, the call when someone goes quiet — you're doing that and calling it logistics. That's building culture, and when it works, people reach each other differently than they would without you in the middle of it. They turn up to each other because you set the tone.

What hasn't happened is the claim on it. Saying once that you want it isn't vanity; it's the plain fact that your hand is on the thing. Other people may know your pleasure in it and you may not. That's the gap worth closing this week: not what you're already doing, but saying so.
cells.sheetLine: You are already keeping this alive. Just claim it once.
cells.handle: Not what you're already doing, but saying so.

attempts.check: Unsupported claim: that 'counting the heads' is already happening to this person — the record gives the mechanism, not their life, and the U cell must offer the claim of running authorship without asserting it landed. A reader could reasonably say 'nobody's counting anything, I just don't go to the party' — the ask still works because putting the old shape to rest is doable regardless of which read is right. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is the celebratory mirror-image — 'joy wants to be shared and you're already the one sharing it' — that flatters the balanced face without evidence.
